title: AI in Education #5: Five Things I Learned from Simon Woodhead
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton distills five takeaways from a conversation with Simon Woodhead, Eedi's Chief Data Scientist and Barton's co-founder of 15 years, about what a decade of diagnostic-question data can actually do now that machine learning has matured. The core insight is that Eedi's distractors were designed from the outset to capture specific misconceptions, so a wrong answer is not just 'wrong' but a precise signal about a student's thinking -- data that sat mostly unused for years until models could exploit it. Eedi's dynamic quiz now uses 10 answered questions to predict how a student would answer hundreds of unseen ones, including which specific wrong distractor they would pick, though Woodhead is candid that any intervention based on a prediction contaminates the ability to test that prediction. He describes two ideas Eedi tried and abandoned a decade ago -- crowd-rated student explanations (killed by students gaming it with obscene keyboard art) and OCR on handwritten/image-based questions -- that are newly viable because NLP moderation and OCR have both improved dramatically. The most reliable AI question-writing workflow keeps a human teacher correcting the AI's draft distractors, with every correction captured as training data. His closing example -- an English phonetic-trap distractor ('twe-' for twelve/twenty) that simply does not exist in Hindi -- illustrates that adapting AI tools to a new market means redesigning the underlying misconception model, not just translating text.
points: Because Eedi's multiple-choice distractors were engineered from the start to capture specific misconceptions, a wrong answer carries precise diagnostic signal, which is what makes a decade of stored response data newly valuable now that models can exploit it.

Eedi's dynamic quiz predicts how a student would answer hundreds of unseen questions -- including which specific distractor -- from just 10 answered questions, but Woodhead flags a genuine self-fulfilling-prophecy problem: once a teacher intervenes on a prediction, the data needed to test that prediction is compromised.

Ideas that failed a decade ago (crowd-rated student explanations killed by students gaming the system with obscene keyboard art; OCR too weak to read handwriting or maths notation) are now viable because NLP moderation and OCR have both improved enough to solve the original blockers.

The most reliable AI question-writing workflow is not fully automated: a teacher edits the AI's draft distractors, and Eedi captures every correction as training data, which threads the needle between Daisy Christodoulou's 10/90 human-AI split and Adam Boxer's worry about deskilling teachers.

Porting an AI education tool to a new market is not a translation problem but a misconception-redesign problem -- a counting question's English-specific phonetic-trap distractors ('twe-' for twelve vs. twenty) simply do not exist in Hindi, so the underlying knowledge graph has to be rebuilt per language and culture.
quotes: Because our distractors are designed to capture specific misconceptions, a student choosing option B is not just “wrong” – it tells you something specific about what they were thinking.
Simon was honest: this is genuinely hard. As he put it, “as soon as you have intervened, you have affected the data.

Yes, kids drew penises using dashes and dots on the keyboard. Other kids liked them. And suddenly, the most popular explanation for quadratic equations was a picture that definitely was not about quadratic equations.

It gets the question stem right. It usually gets two or three of the distractors spot on – distractors that genuinely capture common misconceptions. But it almost always gets at least one distractor wrong.
We cannot use this. None of the distractors work in Hindi. Hindi does not have “teen” numbers – each number in the teens has a unique word.
anyone selling you a one-size-fits-all AI tutoring product for a global market is probably oversimplifying the problem.
